extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, in-house counsel, and patent portfolio managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how to file continuation (and related) patent applications to preserve priority, pursue alternate claim scopes or claim types, manage double-patenting risks, and control costs in a USPTO-filed portfolio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification support for new claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuation application is a new application that claims priority to an earlier application and shares the same disclosure...so long as the spec supports the new claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may pursue different claim scopes years after the original filing without losing the earlier priority date only if the original specification provides support for the new claim language; do not attempt to claim subject matter not supported by the parent disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a continuation pending as an enforcement/response option
rubrics_metrics.description: A pending continuation is an option to write claims that read on a competitor's product as soon as it ships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a competitor releases a feature years after the original filing that was disclosed (even tangentially) in your spec, having a pending continuation allows you to draft claims targeting that feature; once the final patent issues with no pending continuation, that option is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: File the continuation before the parent issues (timing requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: File the continuation while the parent is still pending (typically right before the issue fee is due on the parent). Otherwise you lose continuation rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, the common trick is to file the continuation immediately before the parent's issue fee deadline to preserve continuation rights; missing this window forfeits the ability to file a continuation claiming the parent's priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish CIP vs. continuation vs. divisional (priority and new matter effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuation has the same disclosure as the parent. A continuation-in-part (CIP) adds new matter; new claims supported by the new matter only get the CIP filing date. A divisional pursues claims to subject matter restricted out of the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because CIPs introduce new matter and create complicated priority date issues, many strategists prefer continuations and divisionals when possible; choose the vehicle that preserves desired priority dates and minimizes complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use continuations to shift claim type
rubrics_metrics.description: The parent might claim a method. The continuation can claim the apparatus. A second continuation can claim the computer-readable medium. A third can claim a system of multiple devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting successive continuations to claim different claim categories (method, apparatus, medium, system) lets you reach different potential infringers/defendants; plan claim diversification across continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use continuations to test new legal/theory framings (e.g., 101 technical improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec written in 2020 might support a 101-eligible 'technical improvement' framing that did not feel necessary at the time. A 2027 continuation can pursue claims with that framing if the spec contains the seeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuations allow delayed pursuit of alternative claim theories or eligibility framings as case law or enforcement needs evolve; ensure the original disclosure contains the basis for any later-applied theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for obviousness-type double patenting (OTDP) and terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: When you file multiple applications from the same parent, you may have to file terminal disclaimers to avoid OTDP rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers tie the patent term to the parent's term; be prepared to file them and to accept shortened or tied patent terms where required. Maintain awareness of which applications are subject to OTDP risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track application relationships and terminal-disclaimer ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a tracker of which applications are tied to which.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational practice: maintain a tracker showing which continuations/divisionals/CIPs are linked and which have terminal disclaimers so you can manage term impacts, licensing, and enforcement planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget for continuation practice costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuation costs roughly the same as the original filing in attorney fees plus USPTO fees, but the disclosure is reused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many practitioners budget $5,000–$15,000 per continuation; account for attorney drafting/prosecution costs and USPTO fees even though the specification drafting burden is reduced.
